content: In Aristotelian logic, the Square of Opposition is a diagram that visually represents the logical relationships between four types of categorical propositions. These propositions are classified as follows: 1. The A proposition, known as the universal affirmative, is expressed in Latin as omnis S est P, meaning every S is P. 2. The E proposition, the universal negative, is expressed as nullus S est P, meaning no S is P. 3. The I proposition, the particular affirmative, is expressed as quidam S est P, meaning some S is P. 4. The O proposition, the particular negative, is expressed as quidam S non est P, meaning some S is not P. Aristotle identified specific logical relationships between these propositions. For every affirmative statement, there is a corresponding negation, and these pairs are in direct opposition, meaning one must be true while the other is false. Such pairs are called contradictions. For example, every man is white contradicts not every man is white, and no man is white contradicts some man is white. Statements that are contrary cannot both be true simultaneously. For instance, every man is white and no man is white are contraries because they cannot both be true at the same time. However, they are not contradictions because both can be false. For example, it is false that every man is honest (since some men are not honest), and it is also false that no man is honest (since some men are honest). The opposites of contraries, known as subcontraries, can both be true but cannot both be false. Subcontraries are particular statements, such as some man is just and some man is not just. These statements cannot both be false because their universal contradictory statements (every man is just and no man is just) cannot both be true. Another logical relationship, implied but not explicitly mentioned by Aristotle, is subalternation. This relationship exists between a universal statement and its corresponding particular statement. For example, if every man is white is true, then some man is white must also be true. Similarly, if no man is white is true, then not every man is white must also be true. In summary: Universal statements are contraries. For example, every man is just and no man is just cannot both be true, but they can both be false if at least one man is just and at least one man is not just. Particular statements are subcontraries. For example, some man is just and some man is not just cannot both be false. Universal affirmatives and particular affirmatives are subalternates. For example, every A is B implies some A is B. Universal affirmatives and particular negatives are contradictions. For example, if some A is not B, then not every A is B. In modern interpretations, the semantics of statements like every A is B differ from Aristotelian logic. Modern logic interprets every A is B as for any x, if x is A, then x is B, which does not imply some x is A. This difference in interpretation does not mean Aristotelian logic is incorrect but reflects a difference in semantic frameworks. The medieval logicians represented these relationships in a diagram called the Square of Opposition, with the four propositions placed at the corners of a square and their logical relationships depicted as lines connecting them. A significant issue in Aristotelian logic is the problem of existential import. Subcontraries, such as some A is B and some A is not B, cannot both be false because their universal contradictory statements (every A is B and no A is B) cannot both be true. However, this implies that some A is B presupposes the existence of at least one A. For example, some man is white implies that at least one man exists. But what if men do not exist? This issue was first identified by Peter Abelard, who pointed out that subcontraries with subject terms denoting non-existent entities, such as a man who is a stone, are both false. In the 19th century, George Boole proposed a modern interpretation of the Square of Opposition. He required existential import for particular claims (I and O) but allowed universal claims (A and E) to lack existential import. This adjustment made Venn diagrams particularly useful for term logic and led to the development of the modern Square of Opposition. In this modern version, A and O claims remain contradictory, as do E and I claims, but other forms of opposition, such as contraries, subcontraries, and subalterns, no longer hold. Consequently, modern logic often focuses on the direct opposition of claims rather than the multiple types of oppositions emphasized in traditional Aristotelian logic.
